title: What's the deal with Executive Orders?
summary: Josh and Chuck explain executive orders: what they are, their constitutional basis (Article II), and their history from George Washington through Lincoln's habeas corpus suspension, Teddy Roosevelt, FDR, and Truman's 1952 steel seizure (Youngstown Sheet & Tube v. Sawyer). They cover the Supreme Court's three-tier framework for presidential authority, the ways executive orders can be overturned (judicial review, congressional legislation, veto fights, funding withholding, future presidents rescinding), and modern controversies under Reagan, George W. Bush, Obama (Guantanamo), and Clinton (Balkans). The episode opens with a discussion of a claimed Obama plan to control the economy, referencing Executive Order 13603 (National Defense Resources Preparedness). Closing segments include plugs for a horror fiction contest and San Diego Comic Con, and a listener mail letter from a United Methodist pastor.

segments.title: Opening banter and Obama economic control claim
segments.summary: Hosts chat casually, then discuss a Cato Institute alert claiming Obama planned to take control of the economy via an executive order (13603, National Defense Resources Preparedness), and introduce executive orders as law issued by a president without Congress.

segments.title: Definition and constitutional basis of executive orders
segments.summary: Executive orders defined as directives from a president or governor issued without legislative or judicial input. Presidents cite Article II's executive power vesting and the commander-in-chief and take-care clauses, though the Constitution does not explicitly grant the power to issue them.

segments.title: Early history: Washington, Lincoln and habeas corpus
segments.summary: Washington issued early orders; Nixon-era comparison is made jokingly. Lincoln suspended habeas corpus for John Merryman during the Civil War, and Congress later passed the Habeas Corpus Act. Executive orders were numbered retroactively and later published in the Federal Register from 1962.

segments.title: Teddy Roosevelt and FDR's New Deal orders
segments.summary: Teddy Roosevelt was the first president to exceed a thousand executive orders. FDR issued a large number, starting with closing the banks on day one, creating New Deal industry cartels and the Works Progress Administration, and issuing about 3,500 orders across his terms.

segments.title: Truman's steel seizure and Youngstown ruling
segments.summary: During the Korean War, Truman seized control of steel mills to keep production going during a strike rather than using the Taft-Hartley cooling-off period. The Supreme Court struck it down in Youngstown Sheet and Tube v. Sawyer, and the Court laid out three levels of presidential authority depending on congressional consent.
topics: Youngstown Sheet and Tube v. Sawyer

segments.title: Overturning executive orders and modern controversies
segments.summary: Executive orders can be overturned by judicial review, by Congress passing contrary legislation (subject to veto), by Congress withholding funding, or by a future president rescinding them. Modern examples include Reagan's regulatory cost-benefit orders, George W. Bush's secret wiretapping order, Obama's Guantanamo orders, and Clinton's Balkans actions.

segments.title: Listener mail and plugs
segments.summary: Plugs for a horror fiction contest and the hosts' San Diego Comic Con appearance on July 12, followed by a listener letter from a United Methodist pastor praising the show's handling of faith topics and mentioning Kiva loans. Sign-off.
